## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)
*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*
The *Mahāmaṅgalajātaka* (Ja 453) is a Jātaka tale set at Jetavana, framed by the Buddha in connection with the *Mahāmaṅgala-sutta* (or the Treatise on Omens), opening with the prompt "Declare the truth" [SuttaCentral]. The verses in the text address the nature of auspicious signs (*maṅgala*) and faith. David J. Kalupahana observes that the teaching on practical blessings elucidated in the *Mahāmangala-sutta* and the *Svastyāyana-gāthā* also occurs in the *Mahāmaṅgala-jātaka*, testifying to the antiquity of these traditional blessings [Kalupahana 2001]. Discussing early conceptions of faith (*saddhā*) in canonical Pali literature, B. C. Law notes that the *Mahāmaṅgalajātaka* contains a verse reflecting early Indian notions of religious gift-giving, asserting that food, drink, garlands, perfumes, and unguents offered by the faithful with a contented mind serve as causes of celestial rebirth [Law 1931].
Regarding parallels and textual transmission, B. M. Barua identified chapter 38 of the Chinese *Fa-kheu-king* as a translation of an Indian recension of the *Mahāmaṅgalajātaka* [Barua 1921]. In text-reuse analysis, DharmaNexus records widespread Pali-internal correspondence between the canonical verses and the prose narrative of the *Jātaka-aṭṭhakathā* (Catuttho bhāgo), as well as automatic cross-language alignments with the Sanskrit *Mahāvastu-avadāna* (scoring up to 75) and Kṣemendra's Tibetan *Bodhisattvāvadānakalpalatā* [DharmaNexus].
